articles.title: The club making European history for minnows Andorra
articles.summary: Maurizio Pochettino and inter Club d'Escaldes are set to make European history for footballing minnows Andorra.
articles.body:
The return of the Uefa Conference League may be inconsequential for some, but for Maurizio Pochettino it represents the culmination of a lifelong ambition.

Pochettino spent much of his childhood watching Espanyol, where his father Mauricio - now United States head coach - was first a player and then manager.

As Espanyol reached the 2007 Uefa Cup final, Pochettino dreamed of playing in Europe.

On Thursday, he will realise that ambition when Inter Club d'Escaldes become the first Andorran side to play in the league or group phase of a European competition.

"It feels like it hasn't sunk in yet," Pochettino, 25, tells BBC Sport. "For such a small country, such a small league that isn't known around Europe… it's a dream come true."

Not only is Inter's achievement significant for those involved, but it could prove key for the development of an international football minnow.

Inter made history on a late August evening.

After the first leg of their Conference League play-off against Drita in Kosovo ended 2-2, Inter dominated the return leg without scoring and the tie went to penalties.

Mauricio Pochettino watched from the stands as his son found the bottom corner, before a Drita miss allowed striker Faysal Chouaib to finish the job and spark wild celebrations at Andorra's national stadium.

It was the crowning moment of an extraordinary period in the club's history.

Inter were founded in 1991 and helped form Andorra's top flight four years later, where they remained until relegation in 2015.

They returned to the Primera Diviso under new ownership in 2017 and won their first league title in 2019-20. Five titles in the past seven seasons have emphatically ended the dominance of FC Santa Coloma.

Few people are as synonymous with Andorran football as Ildefons Lima. The former defender represented Andorra for 26 years - the longest international career in men's football history - and leads the nation in appearances (137) and goals (11).

Not only was he part of the boardroom group that oversaw Inter's rise, he helped win titles on the pitch during the final years of his playing career.

"Inter's qualification shows it is possible for people to believe that reaching the final stages of the Conference League is a realistic objective," Lima tells BBC Sport.

Lima stepped away from the club after he retired in 2023, and a year later Felip Ortiz was appointed manager.

After spending much of his life connected with Barcelona as a youth player and later a coach, the 49-year-old instilled a possession-based style which has paid dividends.

"I never thought about it [playing in Europe]," he says. "When you think about it, you don't only think about getting there but also the way you want to get to these competitions.

"Being at Barcelona made me brave in my tactics - I am happy because playing this type of football has helped us achieve our goal."

The Primera Diviso draws limited attention in Andorra, never mind outside its borders. Most locals prefer to watch Andorra FC - the club owned by former Barcelona and Spain defender Gerard Pique that plays in the Spanish second tier.

Several teams share stadiums in Andorra's 10-team top flight, so it's common for matches to take place back-to-back on the same day. Each side plays each other three times, but players end up seeing the same faces every weekend.

"Perhaps the feel of the league is not as professionalised, but the end result can be better than anywhere else," said Pochettino.

After coming up through the academies at Southampton and Tottenham before spending six months at Watford, the defender moved to Spain and played in the semi-professional third and fourth tiers. When the chance to join Inter came about in 2025, the prospect of European football was something he couldn't ignore.

"You have the chance to do something you might not get the chance to do elsewhere," he says. "It was a great decision to come here. More eyes are on you, the spotlight is bigger, it gives you a chance to push on in your career."

Though Pochettino admitted the lack of fans and atmosphere at matches can make the league feel "cold", he believes the competition is progressing.

"The teams in the league are getting more competitive each year because they all have that incentive to play in Europe, which is a financial incentive also. Everyone is pushing, making better teams every year."

Inter are projected to earn over 3m euros (£2.5m) from playing in the league stage - about 2.5 times their annual budget.

Andorra is the 12th nation to have a club qualify for European competition for the first time since the Conference League was introduced in 2021. San Marino and Montenegro are the only Uefa members who have not.

Achievements of this magnitude are unheard of in a nation accustomed to being a punching bag on the international stage.

Andorra is a country of just 90,000 people sandwiched between Spain and France high in the Pyrenees. Unsurprisingly, such a small population and a lack of quality infrastructure have not been conducive to footballing success.

The national team has won just 14 of their 232 games since becoming members of Fifa in 1996, and once went 16 games without scoring.

They are 175th in the Fifa men's world rankings. San Marino (211), Liechtenstein (207) and Gibraltar (201) are the only European nations below them.

But maybe times are changing. Though their ranking is at a nine-year low, the Uefa Nations League has allowed Andorra to play more meaningful games against opponents of a similar level.

Over two years have passed since they conceded five or more goals in one game - a 5-0 defeat by Spain on the eve of Euro 2024 - while in 2025 they only lost 1-0 and 2-0 to England.

Inter's success has propelled Andorra into the top 50 of Uefa's club coefficient rankings, meaning that for the first time, four Andorran clubs will enter the qualifiers for European competitions next summer.

"Hopefully, this can also help Andorran football continue to grow and develop step by step, and show that with the right work and ambition, Andorran clubs can compete at this level," says Lima.

Ortiz agrees, saying: "As a league it's incredible - maybe players who before didn't want to come to our league will come. That will make the league more competitive and help it to grow."

Inter's European adventure begins with a trip to Swedish champions Mjallby on Thursday, before eye-catching ties against 1991 European Cup winners Red Star Belgrade, Champions League regulars FC Copenhagen, and La Liga side Getafe.

"We know it will be a massive challenge playing against some great teams with much bigger budgets than us, but we also believe in ourselves," says Pochettino.

"We've been able to get here so we deserve to be here. We are going to try to show the rest of Europe that we are a team that can make things difficult for the bigger opponents, and that we can get points and belong here."

articles.title: Pepe Brasín sentencia el proyecto del Real Madrid: "O es un punto de inflexión o se acabó este proyecto"
articles.standfirst: El periodista analiza en La Tribu los problemas del equipo de Mourinho, cuestiona la titularidad de Vinicius y señala a Arda Güler como el mejor futbolista del conjunto blanco
articles.summary: El periodista analiza en La Tribu los problemas del equipo de Mourinho, cuestiona la titularidad de Vinicius y señala a Arda Güler como el mejor futbolista del conjunto blanco
articles.body: A pesar de la victoria del Real Madrid ante la Roma en Champions ha vuelto a dejar muchas dudas sobre el proyecto de José Mourinho. Pepe Brasín analizó en La Tribu junto a Pablo Villa los problemas del conjunto blanco y lanzó un contundente aviso sobre el futuro del equipo. Para el periodista, el problema va mucho más allá del entrenador o de determinados futbolistas. "O es un punto de inflexión o se acabó este proyecto. No hay más", respondió Brasín cuando Pablo Villa le preguntó si el partido ante la Roma podía suponer un punto de inflexión. Una reflexión que acompañó de una crítica a la construcción del equipo: "No es una cuestión solo de un entrenador, porque por aquí han pasado cuatro con este mismo grupo; no es cuestión de un solo jugador, porque todos ellos rinden mal cuando juegan juntos; por lo tanto es una cuestión de proyecto, es una cuestión de club". Brasín puso el foco en la incompatibilidad de algunas de las grandes estrellas madridistas. "¿Cuántas pruebas más necesita este club para saber que con Tchouaméni, Valverde como mediocentros, Bellingham de media punta, Mbappé y Vinicius en la delantera, no se funciona? No es un buen equipo, no es un equipo que aspire a ganar la Champions o que aspire a ganar la Liga", aseguró. El periodista insistió en que los problemas se han repetido independientemente del técnico que estuviera en el banquillo: "Da igual que sea Carlo Ancelotti, que sea Xabi Alonso, que sea Arbeloa, que sea Mourinho... ¿Cuánto más necesitan?". Y dejó una de las reflexiones más llamativas de su intervención: "¿Es mejor equipo el Real Madrid con peores jugadores? La respuesta palmaria es que sí. Es que es obvio que sí". Vinicius, al banquillo: "Los cuatro partidos de sanción en la Liga le vienen muy bien al Real Madrid" Preguntado por Pablo Villa sobre qué cambios introduciría en el once, Brasín fue especialmente contundente con Vinicius: "Yo creo que no puede jugar Vinicius ahora mismo. No es solo que no encaje con el resto, que no lo hace". "Creo que Vinicius es el que peor en forma está. No debería ser titular de este equipo. En ese sentido, los cuatro partidos de sanción en la Liga le vienen muy bien a Real Madrid", añadió, reconociendo que su opinión podía resultar sorprendente por la calidad del brasileño. También defendió la sanción impuesta al delantero: "Su actitud entra de lleno en la expulsión, que es justa, y en lo que el reglamento estipula para estos casos. Perfecta". En el apartado de nombres propios, Brasín señaló al futbolista sobre el que debería construirse el equipo: "Guler es imprescindible, es totalmente imprescindible. Fede Valverde no puede jugar en el medio centro". El periodista fue todavía más lejos al valorar el rendimiento del turco: "Es el mejor jugador del Real Madrid ahora mismo. A palo seco. Sumándolo todo, juntándolo todo, lo que hemos visto de temporada, el mejor jugador del Real Madrid es Arda Guller". Por último, abrió otro debate alrededor de Jude Bellingham y su encaje en el ataque madridista: "La pregunta con Bellingham es… ¿Qué es Bellingham en el Real Madrid? ¿Quién es? ¿Y qué tiene que ser? ¿Qué puede ser? Yo no creo que sea mediocampista, yo creo que es delantero".

Vinicius durante el partido frente al Villarreal en el Bernabéu.

articles.title: Fifa: Could Arsene Wenger take on Gianni Infantino for presidency?
articles.summary: Senior figures in European football tell BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run as a surprise candidate against Gianni Infantino.
articles.body:
Despite the backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors, Fifa president Gianni Infantino looks increasingly likely to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next year.

Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run as a surprise candidate.

But would the man who has been the governing body's head of global development since 2019 really challenge his own boss? And what lies behind the support he has?

On Thursday the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since the emergence of Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme plunged the organisation into crisis, leading to calls from the game's leaders in Europe, North America and Asia for him to step down.

A defiant Infantino will come face to face with some of his fiercest critics at what could be a spicy gathering in Zurich.

Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development. But Infantino will also face scrutiny over governance reforms, FFE, the awarding of the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize last year to US President Donald Trump, and disciplinary procedures in the wake of the Folarin Balogun affair.

But the meeting will also bring into sharp focus the failure so far to identify a unifying figure with the worldwide appeal to challenge Infantino.

While potential rivals like Victor Montagliani, the president of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (Concacaf), and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders, Infantino has been busy touring the world, shoring up his position.

The growing expectation is that such is the support he retains in his power base of Africa, South America and Oceania, he will be returned, despite only carrying the backing of roughly half of Fifa's 211 members.

To date, the only person to declare their intention to run is the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although few rate his chances.

Here in Zurich, there is no indication that he is plotting a bid. On Wednesday evening Wenger joined Infantino and other Fifa Council members for dinner in a Zurich restaurant. As a senior member of Fifa's management team, he will also be present at Thursday's meeting.

When BBC Sport asked about his intentions via Fifa, no comment was provided.

Meanwhile, those close to the 76 year-old, who left Arsenal in 2018 after 22 years in which he became the most successful manager in the club's history, will not be drawn on whether he is interested.

One told BBC Sport he would be "an ideal candidate, but he is his own man".

What is clear is that he does have supporters, who believe he commands the level of respect beyond Europe that would be essential if the Uefa-led rebellion against Infantino is to have any chance of success.

"He isn't a football politician, but it would bring football and integrity to the leadership of Fifa" says Alex Phillips, a former Uefa and Fifa executive told the BBC.

"It's become way too much focused on money and not enough focused on football. And I think someone like that would put football back as the main priority. Let's see what he decides. There may be other candidates as well."

A current senior official at a European national association agrees that Wenger "truly understands football development because he's been running it.

"People don't see him as just a European. He's very respected in Asia, for instance, from his time working in Japan. A lot of people are saying he'd be the ideal candidate. With him, it's not about money, status or ego. He genuinely loves the game.

"He's made a difficult role work and understands Fifa, and that's why he'd be a really good candidate.

"That said, he's in a really difficult position."

That was highlighted amid the fallout over FFE, when Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said in a statement at the time. "The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."

Some may have expected Wenger to resign over the controversy, given his thinly veiled criticism of Infantino, the way he had been kept in the dark, and the condemnation of the plot from stakeholders across the game. But he has carried on in a role in which he oversees youth development at academies in 60 countries, as well as youth competitions around the world. He is also a technical adviser to rule-making body International Football Association Board (Ifab).

Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups , and the idea of a 'daylight' offside law.

But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.

Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent.

Indeed, at the weekend Wenger was in Cape Verde at a Confederation of African Football conference, telling the delegates: "We want to see an African team win the World Cup, and the numbers show that it is feasible."

Such sentiments would do him no harm if he was to stand for president.

BBC Sport has been told that a large number of Fifa's staff also want Wenger to run, and believe he could change the organisation's image.

Others, however, are more sceptical. One well-connected figure in Fifa circles told BBC Sport that he would be "amazed if Wenger would rise up against the man who appointed him in the first place. Arsene has had some fairly 'out there' ideas. In terms of the administration of the game and the relationships on a political level, in the kind of places you're going to need to corral and command power, I'm not sure he's the man for that."

Another senior European official said: "He has the stature, but I'm not sure he smacks of the future. Maybe he could do a single term to introduce reforms. He is very respected in the game and has done a good job of the development programmes, but whether he'd split from Gianni, I just don't know."

If Wenger does want to run, he has until 18 November to declare his candidacy, and would need to be nominated by at least five national associations.

As a manager, Wenger is remembered as a legendary figure who changed English football with his forward-thinking approach to tactics and nutrition.

Could he attempt a shake-up of a different kind at Fifa? It is an intriguing prospect.

articles.summary: In an exclusive interview with Sky Sports' Sam Blitz, Brentford midfielder Mamadou Sangare reveals why he turned down bigger clubs in Europe to join the Bees; the Mali international believes Brentford are capable of finishing in the top four this season - even the top two...
articles.body:
Not only did the midfielder star for RC Lens last season - playing a key role as they finished as Ligue 1 runners-up and French Cup champions - but there were major European clubs eyeing up his signature over the summer.

And not just major clubs, the elite of the elite. Yet he turned those bigger clubs down for a Brentford team without European football this season.

"Yeah it's true," he tells Sky Sports from Brentford's training ground about that interest. "But I'm not going to give any names, out of respect.

"There were a lot of clubs. For me, the most important thing was to know where I could progress. And Brentford was the best place for my development.

"A coach who really wanted me was something that was important to me. That's why I chose Brentford."

It is fair to say Sangare had earned a big move. As well as his club success with Lens, he was also named in the Ligue 1 Team of the Year at the age of 24, pipping Paris Saint-Germain duo Joao Neves and Fabian Ruiz to a midfield spot.

So was it hard to say no to some of the major European clubs? "No, it wasn't difficult," he replies.

"Just because a big club comes calling, it doesn't mean you have to say yes to it. You have to see a lot of different aspects.

"I'm a little different from other players because I see things differently. For me, Brentford was the best option - as a young player, as a player who still has to prove himself at a high level.

"I think that choosing Brentford was the best option for me to progress and to reach my best potential."

'I'd never seen an approach like that' - Sangare on Brentford's pitch to him

If Sangare wasn't a coup for Brentford when he joined, he was definitely one after his Premier League debut. He got two assists as the Bees hammered Tottenham on the opening weekend, but the way he strutted around with ease in his first Premier League game made him a star for the future already.

"He can play for a top four club," said Jamie Redknapp after that display. And the big question everyone had was: how do Brentford keep on spotting then securing future gems in the making?

The key is in the preparation when it comes to Brentford, who pitch the club to incoming players via a very detailed presentation.

Bryan Mbeumo recently revealed how thorough Brentford's pitch can be. The Bees watched him 28 times for Ligue 2 side Troyes before approaching him in 2019, then presented him with all his strengths and weaknesses on a screen.

Because of this presentation, he had a clear idea of where he'd fit in, where he'd improve - and seven years later, he was sold to Manchester United for £71m. He had gone from a French second-division player to scoring 20 Premier League goals in a single season for the Bees.

And for Sangare? "It was exactly the same," he says about the presentation that Brentford gave him over the summer.

"It was incredible. It was the first time I've ever seen something like that. I've been at a few clubs, but I've never seen an approach like that.

"Brentford has a well-placed structure. It was something I've never seen before - it really pushed me to choose this club.

"I had a positive, detailed discussion with the coach. He showed me his style of play and what he expected from me.

"He also showed me the tools which could allow me to improve. He showed me my weaknesses and what I needed to work on. I'm a young player, I really liked that.

"When a coach speaks to you like that, it shows that he wants to see you improve. It was really important for me."

However, not all roads are straightforward in football. Despite being the new darling of Brentford, he has started the last two games against Chelsea and Aston Villa on the bench.

There is no injury. Instead, he is competing with the trustworthy pair of long-term servants Vitaly Janelt and Mathias Jensen for a midfield starting spot. Yehor Yarmoliuk is another up and coming option in that position and scored at Villa. Sangare has had to wait his turn after such a high-profile start.

"I haven't spoken much about that with the coach," Sangare says about his recent appearances on the bench. "He's the coach, he's the boss. I'm a player like so many others. It's not only about me here.

"The most important thing is the team. That's what counts. Whether I start or not, as long as they need me, I'll be there.

"It's up to me to work even harder to get my place back, even though I wouldn't say that I lost it. It's up to me to keep working and to do even more than the others. We'll see how it goes."

Despite his limited appearances in recent weeks, Sangare has still shown his worth. He averages the most tackles out of any Premier League player per 90 minutes, while only Man City's Elliot Anderson has won more duels on the ground than the Mali midfielder.

With the calibre of player like Sangare in the team, it makes Brentford such a hard team to beat. They are still unbeaten in the Premier League this season, having beaten Chelsea and Tottenham and drawn with Aston Villa.

Liverpool are up next at the Gtech Community Stadium on Saturday, having been stung by Keith Andrews' side in this fixture last season. Even though they have never played a European match before, Brentford are a continental club in the making.

'Why can't Brentford reach top four, or top two?'

Sangare managed to defy all the odds at Lens last season, taking them to Europe and winning them a cup. That would be the perfect tonic for Brentford fans this season - who have never won a major trophy in their history.

But with Brentford sitting fourth in the table after six games, Sangare's message is clear: Europe is not enough.

"The goal is to reach Europe and win as many games as possible," he says. "We know that Brentford has never played a European game before.

"Why can't we also reach the top four, or the top two? Why can't we cause a real surprise? Because we're a good team in the league. We have a very good team with very good players, with a great coach as well."

Those are the team's ambitions. What about his own? After his performances for Brentford already this season, many have branded him as the next player off the conveyer belt, after the Bees brought in nearly £200m for Mbeumo, Yoane Wissa, Ivan Toney and David Raya.

"I saw some comments about that," says Sangare about transfer rumours linking him with a move away already. "I don't think too much about it. I just want to work and help the team to reach their goals.

"They put a lot of money in me. They trusted me. It's up to me to do everything to make it happen - by winning games, by improving the team.

"These are the things I have to put in my head, not transfers or anything like that. I have to focus on the team. This is what we have to do. Win games and improve the team by getting our goals."

articles.title: Messi’s Inter Miami beat New York City to reach third straight MLS playoff
articles.summary: Messi assist sets Inter Miami on way to 2-0 win against New York City FC as back-to-back wins guarantee playoff place.
articles.body:
Lionel Messi set up a Rodrigo De Paul goal, and German Berterame snapped his scoring drought as Inter Miami booked their place in the MLS (Major League Soccer) playoffs with a 2-0 win over New York City FC on Wednesday.

Victory gave Cristian “Kily” Gonzalez his first back-to-back wins since taking over as head coach last month, guaranteeing second-placed Miami at least a place in the wild card round of the competition in the United States, with five games left to play.

“I’m leaving happy. Obviously, there’s a lot to improve, but we’re making progress little by little,” Gonzalez said.

Messi – who had scored twice on Saturday after returning to his club side from last week’s emotional Argentina send-off – was again a dangerous presence, playing a hand in both first-half goals.

In the 20th minute, Messi trapped the ball just outside the penalty area and passed it to De Paul, who found Suarez on the byline with a diagonal looping ball.

Suarez rolled it flat across the face of the goal, giving Berterame a simple finish for his first goal since May.

De Paul grabbed Miami’s second on a quick counter with the final kick of the first half. Berterame brought the ball across the halfway line and was slightly fortunate to find Messi to his right with a mishit pass.

Messi drew in three defenders then laid it off with the outside of his left foot to De Paul, who slammed it high to the keeper’s right.

In a goalless second half, Messi sent a curling effort from just outside the box over the bar.

As the game clock hit 90, Messi played a short corner to De Paul, who unleashed a shot from outside the box towards the far top corner. United States national team goalkeeper Matt Freese made a superb diving save, tipping the ball onto the post.

New York City, on a dire streak of just one win in their last 11 MLS games, at least had a chance for a consolation deep in stoppage time with a penalty.

Ian Fray brought down fellow substitute Talles Magno, who turned sharply away from goal and ran into the defender’s trailing leg.

But Dayne St Clair made a brilliant save, flinging himself low and right to palm the ball around the bar.

It was Inter Miami’s second straight clean sheet, after none in their previous 10.

“I really liked how we handled dropping back into defensive shape. We didn’t get caught out on the counter and were very aggressive, breaking up plays whenever a sudden transition from them looked likely,” said Gonzalez.

“Perhaps our ball circulation was a bit too slow at times, but that’s just how the game played out.”

Even with first-place Nashville out of sight this year in the Eastern Conference, the win consolidated Miami’s grip on second and home-field advantage into the playoffs.

images.caption: Inter Miami's Argentinian forward Lionel Messi, flanked by Brazilian defender Casemiro, applauds after win in New York City FC [Chandad Khanna/AFP]

articles.title: Man United’s Martinez takes to social media to defend his criticism of club
articles.summary: Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez follows up criticism of his club with social media explanation of frustration.
articles.body:
Manchester United defender Lisandro ‌Martinez has defended his criticism of the club’s leadership following ⁠Tuesday’s 2-0 Champions ⁠League defeat against Atletico Madrid, saying his comments reflected his desire to see the team compete for major honours.

The Argentina international ⁠acknowledged on Wednesday that frustration had shaped his post-match remarks , in which he called for greater investment in the squad and questioned director of football Jason Wilcox’s ⁠recruitment efforts, but stopped short of apologising.

“After the match, I spoke out of anger and frustration at not getting the result we all wanted,” Martinez wrote on Instagram.

“Those who know me know how I live football, with ‌passion, commitment and a huge desire to win. And when things don’t go our way, it hurts, especially when representing a club with the history and stature of Manchester United.

“My words reflect how I feel and how much I want to see this club competing for the biggest honours.”

Martinez reiterated that the players also had to take responsibility for improving ⁠the team’s performances.

“I know that, first and foremost, it’s ⁠us, the players, who have to deliver, and I put myself at the front of that responsibility,” he said. “We need to demand even more of ourselves and work together to take ⁠Manchester United back to the top.”

The defeat extended United’s winless run to five matches in all competitions, adding ⁠to the scrutiny surrounding head coach Michael Carrick ⁠as the club adjusts to life back in the Champions League after two seasons away.

“I believe in my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward,” Martinez ‌added. “I’m convinced that the way forward is to keep working together, with ambition and commitment.”

United have not publicly ‌responded ‌to Martinez’s remarks, although ESPN and Sky Sports reported that Wilcox retained the backing of the club’s leadership.

The club’s manager, Michael Carrick, is due to speak to the media on Friday in his news conference before Sunday’s league match at Leeds United.

articles.title: Liverpool: Graeme Souness rejected Barcelona to join Sampdoria
articles.summary: Liverpool legend Graeme Souness reveals he rejected the chance to sign for Barcelona when he left the European champions.
articles.body:
Liverpool legend Graeme Souness has revealed he rejected the chance to sign for Barcelona when he left the European champions in 1984.

The Scotland midfielder joined Italian club Sampdoria for £650,000 just weeks after lifting Liverpool's fourth European Cup against Roma.

Souness was then one of the world's finest midfielders - he finished sixth in that year's Ballon d'Or - so his decision to swap Anfield for Genoa, rather than one of Europe's heavyweights, was a surprise.

"I had to leave Liverpool because my wife at the time was about to inherit money and she had to spend three years out of the country," Souness told BBC Scotland's The Saturday Show.

"I could have got around it somehow, but I decided to go because at that time Italy was the place to go. All the best players in the world were going there.

"I got offered a two-year deal at Barcelona, which I turned down because I needed three and, even because of my age, go to the third year.

"There were a couple of other clubs in Italy interested, but Sampdoria had been bought by Paolo Mantovani and he was building a young team so wanted an experienced player. That's how I ended up there."

After rejecting Barcelona - who had just appointed Terry Venables as manager and allowed Diego Maradona to leave for Napoli - Souness won an Italian Cup in two seasons at Sampdoria before joining Rangers as player-manager in 1986.

He revolutionised the Ibrox club in a trophy-laden five-year spell in charge and has advised the club on managerial appointments in recent years.

However, he says he would never become Rangers manager again - in the same way as Martin O'Neill has returned to Celtic - because his abrasive style of management does not work with today's players.

"No, Martin's a very different personality to me. He's a nice guy," added the 73-year-old.

"I started in management at 33 and football was a very different workplace then. My style of management, maybe my style of telling people too readily what they don't want to hear, it wouldn't work today.

"Football certainly needs a bit of that, but would it accept it? I doubt it."

'Rangers have planted seed in Celtic's head'

Souness, whose new book 'My Rangers: How I changed Scottish football for ever' was released this week, believes his old club have the psychological edge over Celtic following the two Old Firm victories by Derek McInnes' side in September.

Rangers beat Celtic 3-0 in the League Cup at Ibrox then won 1-0 at Celtic Park in the Premiership a week later and sit two points behind the champions in the table.

"They've now psychologically planted a seed in Celtic's heads that they are bigger, stronger and better than them in the last two games," he said.

"Celtic have left Ibrox after losing 3-0 in the first game thinking, 'how did that happen?' It didn't flatter Rangers.

"So, seven days later, if you're a Celtic supporter, player or on the staff you're thinking 'that won't happen again'. Well, it did happen again, and on your pitch - and the 1-0 did not flatter Rangers.

"So they've now got a psychological edge over Celtic, but that could be short-lived if Rangers were to lose a game against a team they're expected to beat.

"They've given themselves a platform. They're in a wonderful position, but they have to understand that, every team you play, it's the opposition's cup final. So Derek's got to remind them of that and they'll look like they've started to believe.

"Derek has been a player there and knows the Scottish scene. So he was well suited and a great choice. He did get off to a slow start, but in the last couple of games they've turned an enormous corner."

articles.title: Hidalgo avisa: “Luis Castro viene haciendo un gran trabajo. Tienen mucha energía y son muy dinámicos”
articles.standfirst: El técnico del Deportivo estima que el Levante es un equipo muy sólido
articles.summary: Pendientes de la vuelta de Stefan Bajcetic
articles.body: Antonio Hidalgo aseguró esta mañana que el Levante es un equipo muy rocoso y sólido que sabe a lo que quiere jugar. “Es un equipo que busca atraerte mucho, tener un inicio con balón y luego tener mucha gente en la última línea. Habrá que estar muy ajustados y tener esa dosis de paciencia para encontrar los momentos de presión y luego tratar de hacerles daño porque también tienen sus puntos débiles”. El técnico del Deportivo no está preocupado por los goles encajados en todos los partidos de Liga. “En el fútbol moderno ya no es tanta gente la que deja la portería a cero. Tengo una conciencia clara de lo que es la Primera División. Tenemos que estar más ajustados porque, concediendo poco, estamos encajando más de lo que se espera”, comentó. Hidalgo está feliz por ver como jugadores de la clase de Yeremay o la potencia de Adama están cada día mejor y gracias al parón ganaron días. “Adama ha tenido ese inconveniente de no hacer pretemporada, se va encontrando mejor físicamente, el parón le ha venido fenomenal. Va entendiendo lo que le pedimos con y sin balón. Es un proceso y veremos cuándo decidimos ponerlo de inicio. En relación a Yeremay tiene que seguir empujando su límite y nosotros estaremos detrás para darle cariño y exigirle, nos da mucho en última línea rival”

articles.title: Mourinho marca el terreno
articles.standfirst: Eleva el tono a diez días del Clásico
articles.summary: Eleva el tono a diez días del Clásico
articles.body: Dos meses se ha tomado Mourinho para dar el paso al frente, para colocarse en la posición de portavoz del Real Madrid. En un club sin voces desde los despachos, el entrenador se ha convertido en el vehículo de expresión de la entidad. Lo fue Carlo Ancelotti, con su estilo reposado y sus dardos calculados, durante su segunda etapa. En ella apareció el Caso Negreira. Xabi Alonso y Arbeloa no encajaron en ese papel, uno por defecto y otro por exceso. Y ahora Mourinho recupera una labor que ya desarrolló entre 2010 y 2013, cuando alguna vez alzó la voz para quejarse de la soledad que sentía como voz única del club. Después de dos meses de respuestas medidas, calculadas, dejando puertas abiertas, la rueda de prensa en el Olímpico de Roma entró en la despensa de aquellas de las preguntas por los árbitros. El amago tras el derbi dio un paso más. Mourinho puso sobre la mesa palabras gruesas para denunciar la forma en la que dio a conocer la sanción a Vinicius y el hecho de jugar en Atenas el 4 de noviembre y en Mestalla el 7. Lo que eran insinuaciones, como la referencia a que el árbitro designado se conozca semanas antes y no las 24 horas estipuladas, pasaron a ataques frontales. "El madridismo no es estúpido y yo voy a hablar para que se vean las cosas que pasan", aseveró en Roma. Es un llamamiento al Bernabéu para que, como ya se vio ante el Villarreal, muestre que está en sintonía con su entrenador. El partido del domingo, ante el Sevilla, será otra olla a presión contra los árbitros, LaLiga y la Federación. Esa labor de voz del club no es nueva para Mourinho. La ha desarrollado en todos los clubes por los que ha pasado, desde su breve etapa inicial en el Benfica a la previa al Madrid, el Fenerbahçe. Allá donde ha estado ha dejado ruedas de prensa para la posteridad, batallas contra rivales y estamentos que han tenido ocupada a la prensa durante semanas. En Roma, Mourinho entró a fondo en el caso Negreira. Sin decirlo de manera abierta, puso sobre la mesa su idea de que el Barcelona merece un castigo deportivo. Y para ello puso como ejemplo a Italia y el descenso de la Juventus en 2006: "Solo una cosa te digo, enhorabuena a los italianos, ¿sabes por qué? Porque es el único país donde el ‘Calciopoli' ha sido 'Calciopoli’. Porque en España lo que ha pasado, y todos saben lo que ha pasado y parece que todavía no se respira muy bien. Hasta ahora no ha pasado nada. No ha pasado nada. Si no pasa nada es quizás el escándalo más grande de corrupción del arbitraje mundial". No hace falta ser Einstein para saber qué contenido tiene esa denuncia. En apenas diez llega el Clásico. Mourinho ha dado un paso al frente en su discurso. No es de los que reculan y retractan. El alto voltaje para la vosita del Madrid al Camp Nou está asegurado.

articles.title: Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia could be postponed by a year amid Houthi attacks
articles.summary: The tournament is scheduled to begin on January 7 but could be moved by a year if needed, AFC president says.
articles.body:
Football’s Asian Cup, hosted by Saudi Arabia, could be moved back a year to 2028 following a series of attacks on the country by Yemen’s Houthis.

The continental tournament will be rescheduled “if we need to” but the organisers are in “no hurry” to make a decision, Asian Football Confederation President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa said on Thursday.

The 2027 Asian Cup is supposed to kick off on January 7 in the Saudi cities of Jeddah, Riyadh and al-Khobar.

The kingdom has in recent days come under sustained attack in a dramatic escalation from the Houthis.

“We can wait until the end of November,” Al Khalifa told reporters in Zurich on Wednesday about a decision on the fate of the Asian Cup.

“Things can change very quickly for better or worse in the region, and it is a question of seeing what happens,” he added.

“If we need to make a decision then we will, but we could move back a year to 2028 if we need to.

“But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything is on schedule.”

Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr saw their Asian Champions League match delayed by an hour on Monday after Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence said it had intercepted a missile fired towards Riyadh.

Three matches in Saudi domestic football, including one involving Al-Nassr, were postponed this week.

The exhibition Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, due to include Novak Djokovic, Carlos Alcaraz and Alexander Zverev, was pushed back to the end of December.

Australia, one of the 24 teams set to play at the Asian Cup, said this week it was “closely monitoring” the situation in Saudi Arabia.

The organisation representing South Korean players on Thursday said there was “serious concern regarding the safety of all players participating in the Asian Cup”.

“The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that cannot be taken lightly,” said Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, according to the country’s Yonhap News Agency.

Lee added that “no tournament’s value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans.”

images.caption: The previous edition of the AFC Asian Cup was held in Qatar in 2024, when the hosts successfully defended their title [Molly Darlington/Reuters]

articles.title: FIFA set for rule change after Balogun red card row at the World Cup: reports
articles.summary: The governing body’s council is expected to prohibit disciplinary committees from overturning match suspensions.
articles.body:
Football’s global governing body is expected to change a rule that allowed a red card for USA forward Folarin Balogun to be controversially overturned during the World Cup, according to media reports on the agenda for Thursday’s FIFA council meeting in Zurich.

The decision-making body is convening for the first time since this year’s tournament, and a ⁠⁠motion to prohibit such actions in the future will be top of the agenda. Members will also discuss the organisation’s funding, rules and other matters amid a turbulent time in the sport.

During the World Cup’s round-of-32 match, Balogun received a red card for stepping awkwardly on the right ankle of Tarik Muharemovic of Bosnia in a 2-0 win for the home team. It triggered an automatic one-game suspension.

However, United States President Donald Trump urged FIFA President Gianni Infantino to review the case, and Balogun’s red card was overturned, allowing him to play in the USA’s round-of-16 match against Belgium.

The decision to overturn Balogun’s red card ignited one of the tournament’s biggest controversies, with widespread criticism from football federations, former FIFA officials, experts and coaches.

The 37-member FIFA council is expected to vote on whether to prohibit disciplinary committees from overturning automatic match suspensions at the World Cup, but the Balogun controversy is unlikely to go away.

FIFA Vice President Debbie Hewitt is among the sport’s leaders who have asked ‌‌‌‌Infantino to release all documents related to the case.

Thursday’s FIFA council meeting is the first since Infantino came ‌‌‌‌under ‌‌‌‌fire earlier this year for a now-shelved plan to sell a 20 percent stake in the World Cup’s commercial business to private investors.

Infantino has faced calls to resign from the leaders of three regional football confederations – UEFA (Europe), AFC (Asia) ⁠⁠⁠⁠and CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) – and their representatives will be present in Zurich for the FIFA meeting.

They will be joined by their counterparts from Africa, South America and Oceania.

On the agenda will be a discussion of the failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, which Infantino was forced to abandon ⁠⁠⁠⁠within days of announcing it in July.

Under the plan, Infantino proposed selling a minority stake in a FIFA commercial subsidiary to private investors, with a company launched by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, identified as the proposed lead investor.

The council will also address FIFA’s governance, with some of the sport’s most powerful figures determined to limit Infantino’s powers if they cannot force him out of office.

Infantino, 56, will stand for re-election in March 2027, with a ‌‌‌‌November 18 deadline looming for potential candidates to submit their nominations.

articles.title: Omer Riza interview: Ex-Cardiff manager on assisting Ashley Cole in Italy, being banned in Turkey and what drives him on
articles.summary: From his early days at Arsenal to his adventures with Trabzonspor in Turkey, managing Cardiff City in the Championship and assisting Ashley Cole at Cesena in Italy, Omer Riza reflects on a life in football - and what will come next - in this exclusive interview with Sky Sports...
articles.body:
Over the course of an evening, the former Cardiff City boss opens up about many of them. The highs and lows of managing in the Championship, how he once received a global ban from football, and even a recent broken ankle in a charity game. "Silly tackle!"

As a player, he started out at Arsenal, his connection to Cole dating back to when they were just boys. But his league debut came in the Netherlands on loan at Den Haag and he later spent five years in Turkey, including playing European football for Trabzonspor.

As a coach, he has worked with England's age-group sides and managed Cardiff City in the Championship. Cesena was a chance to get back on the grass. "I had that hunger to get going again." Now, after that adventure, he is eager to return to the Football League.

"Italy was a good opportunity, working with Ashely who I have known for so long, and getting to experience a different style of football. The target at Cesena was to change the approach, change the mentality, and that is what we did in a short space of time."

Riza explains: "Italy can be quite defensively minded, low blocks and counter-attacks. They are quite happy not to have the ball. Our mentality was to try to have the ball, to control the game, to provoke the opposition to open up spaces further up the pitch.

"The players were used to a 5-3-2 and defending their box so to go press high and step on to the opposition to stop them playing and win it right up the pitch to cause them problems, that was a big change, not just for the players but for the fans as well."

Cole decided to call time on the Cesena project in the summer when it became clear that the club's ambitions did not match his own. "I honestly believe we would have done really well this year if we had been allowed to bring in the players we wanted," says Riza.

But he is backing his old pal to succeed somewhere else. "He has worked hard at his coaching, he is diligent and he has his head screwed on." Assisting him in the next role is an option. "We have spoken about it." But Riza's real aim is to be a head coach again.

His first taste of it came at Leyton Orient back in 2017. That was no gentle introduction. "There were five managerial changes that season. The owners were not paying the players and the fans were up in arms. It was really tough." But he saw out the season.

Now 46, there have been so many obstacles since. "I applied for hundreds of jobs after that and finally found a job with Watford. I started part-time on £20 an hour and worked my way up from the under-15s to become first-team assistant. And then I got sacked."

That one still grates. It was "a kick in the behind" to discover that his future was tied to departing head coach Valerien Ismael who had only been brought in that summer. "I had been there for five years, I was a Pro Licence coach." But Riza had to start over again.

At Cardiff, in the autumn of 2024, he was trusted with the top job on a caretaker basis after Erol Bulut was dismissed for taking one point from the first six games of the season. The turnaround under Riza was swift and impressive enough to be given the job permanently.

"I got nominated for manager of the month," he recalls. The first of two such nominations in five months. "Taking over after a start like that, it is like you have been deducted points. You are trying to survive. We nearly managed it." Unfortunately, a dip in the spring saw him sacked with three games to go, just one point from safety.

"It became harder to play with freedom and we drew 15 games, too many." Cardiff won none of the three games after he left and they finished bottom of the Championship, despite the fact that they were 19th during the 37-game period that he was in charge.

There are fond memories. A 5-0 win over Plymouth. "Wayne Rooney was in charge then." And two draws with Coventry. "I went up against Frank Lampard, who I played with at West Ham. It was nice to do that." But the derby win over Swansea remains bitter-sweet.

This is the unseen side of the game. "I was up and down the motorway because it was, 'It is your dad, you need to come back.' I would go and sit with my dad until two or three in the morning and then need to be back ready for training the next morning."

That could be a three-hour drive. "It was a very emotional period but I just love what I do and my father would have wanted me to carry on. It was tough but I just knew that." Cardiff beat Swansea 3-0 that weekend. "To get that result for the fans, it was special."

There is pride at the players that he helped to develop. "Yousef Salech is doing very well now. Will Alves and Sivert Mannsverk also did well when they came in." But he accepts that mistakes were made too. Calling out the fans for their criticism is a regret.

"It is not just about what you do on the grass," Riza points out. "You are representing the football club. That is so important. I have learned a lot from the experience, massively. But then, I have had so many different experiences now as a player and as a coach."

How have those experiences shaped his ideas about the game? As a youngster, he was coached by the great Don Howe at Arsenal, often hailed as a visionary. "He was very good at establishing what exactly you were good at as a player and developing it."

There was a season training with the first-team at Arsenal, working up close with Arsene Wenger. The Gunners boss did not say too much but every morsel of information was taken in. "When you get that one little moment of detail, it can sink in a bit deeper."

At Turkey, he added to his knowledge. "I remember our full-backs stepping into holding midfield." This was years before Pep Guardiola popularised the tactic. Those seasons with Trabzonspor brought some of the best moments of his career - and the worst.

"Playing in Europe was a highlight." There is an image of him with his top off celebrating a goal in the UEFA Cup. "As a Turkish-Cypriot, scoring against APOEL, a Greek-Cypriot side, was a fairytale story, really." But his time at Trabzonspor ended on a sour note.

"I ended up getting banned for five months. I left because they had not paid me but the Turkish Federation found me guilty. I had a ten-year battle in the courts, CAS, FIFA, European Court of Human Rights. I won the case but I did not win the pecuniary damages."

The experience damaged his career and his finances. "I spent a lot of money trying to get that but I have helped other people along the way. They had to change the rules. It was a long and painful process and my dad had to go through that too, all my family."

His playing career was not quite the same after that. "No one would sign me because the ban would kick in." He did play on down the pyramid. "That is just how it unravelled." But he considered working in another industry, walking away from the game that he loved.

"In my mind, I was going to come out of football. I remember telling my dad I did not want to do it anymore. But he reminded me I had been doing it since I was six years old, travelling all over the world, so I should try to stay in football. It just progressed from there."

Inspired by his father, and perhaps driven by a player career that did not quite deliver all that it had promised, Riza continues to push for the next opportunity. "It has all made me stronger, made me more resilient," he explains. "I am more than ready for the next chapter."

articles.title: Expert CFB Locks, Predictions for Ohio State vs. Indiana and Week 7's Biggest Games
articles.summary: Behold one of the deepest, most compelling college football slates of the season.
articles.body:
Behold one of the deepest, most compelling college football slates of the season.

From critical conference games to multiple matchups featuring top 10 teams, Week 7 has plenty to offer. And we shall embrace it in full.

We didn't capitalize on last week's opportunities. A strong Week 5 gave way to an extremely "meh" Week 6. There were some highs, although there were more lows. Rather than dwell on it, we're turning the page and trusting the process.

We won't waste any time diving into the meat of this glorious lineup of games. Let's begin.

What a matchup—and its outcome will carry enormous significance as we move through October. The winner will put itself in tremendous shape to win the Big Ten and go well beyond.

Indiana was able to keep its record clean last week with a tremendous come-from-behind win at Nebraska. The Cornhuskers dominated time of possession, controlling the ball for 39 minutes. Still, Indiana manufactured enough offense (and pressure) late in the game.

A bit of a lackluster showing against Nebraska could prompt plenty to back the Buckeyes. They still have Jeremiah Smith, Julian Sayin and plenty of talented players up and down the lineup; it makes sense.

But Indiana showcased incredible resolve—and adjustments—against a much-improved Nebraska group. In particular, quarterback Josh Hoover played an outstanding, clean game.

At home, Indiana will be a different beast entirely after spending the last few games away. Expect a heavy dose of rushes and enough passing, although this doesn't feel like a touchdown fest for either team.

This feels like a field goal game either way, and the hook could loom large.

While the previous game might not be a touchdown fest, this one should produce fireworks.

Ole Miss currently owns the nation's No. 108 scoring defense. And if you watched the Rebels play, this checks out. Missouri is currently No. 29 in the same category, which isn't terrible but isn't dazzling either.

Playing on the road, however, could present some issues for the Tigers. In their last away game, at Mississippi State, things spiraled out of control late.

This, unquestionably, will be the Tigers' toughest road test this season. And while running back Jamal Roberts should find success against a defense that has struggled against the run, the environment coupled with the opposing QB won't be as easy to conquer.

Somehow, Trinidad Chambliss is flying under the radar these days. The loss to Florida took some wind out of his sails, but this could bring that momentum right back.

For as good as Missouri has been, Chambliss is still the best player on this football field—and on most football fields, for that matter.

Going up against Austin Simmons, the QB he once backed up (and replaced) a season ago, Chambliss will showcase just how dominant he can be yet again.

A strong start, albeit against lesser opponents, was derailed over the past two games for James Franklin. If that sounds familiar, well, we get it.

Virginia Tech lost to Pitt and Cal, which has put a damper on his debut season. This week, however, the Hokies are positioned to rebound.

Georgia Tech deserves plenty of credit for beating Duke outright last week. It's been a disappointing season for the Yellow Jackets, which have losses against Colorado and Stanford thus far.

For at least one game, all was well. But having to play on the road in a challenging environment should be a different assignment entirely. The Hokies have better weapons on offense, even if the past few games have produced mixed results.

We're not overthinking this. We're also not overreacting to either team over the past few weeks. At home, Virginia Tech gets right in a major way.

We had Washington last week. We could have ripped that ticket up after about 10 minutes; that's how long it took for Iowa to essentially take over.

On the flip side, we also bet Purdue against Minnesota. The Boilermakers cruised to a 41-13 victory over Minnesota, running for 305 yards along the way.

Complicating matters further is the fact that Washington will likely be starting its backup quarterback. With Demond Williams Jr. injured, Elijah Brown could get the call.

The good news? Brown actually played well when thrust into action against Iowa. In many ways, the offense looked much more functional with him running the show. It hasn't worked of late; something new is needed.

Indeed, the Huskies have lost three consecutive games. All is not well. But given the challenging schedule of late, it wouldn't be shocking to see Washington respond on the road.

Like the game before, we backed this team a week ago. And just like Washington, things didn't go exactly great for West Virginia.

Arizona clobbered the Mountaineers 52-31. Needless to say, we didn't win that bet.

West Virginia ultimately gained more than 500 yards, including 303 rushing yards. If there is any consolation heading into this game, Cincinnati also lost decisively to Arizona, falling 34–7 two weeks earlier.

It's been an interesting year for the Mountaineers, winners of their first three games and losers of the last three. Offensively, things are solid. WVU is averaging more than 36 points per game. Defensively? Well, West Virginia is allowing more than 32 points per game, which is less than ideal.

As for the Bearcats, the 4-1 record feels a little misleading. Even the win over Kansas State doesn't exactly jump off the page these days, and the rest of the schedule doesn't ooze excellence.

With the total hovering around 63, a high-scoring game is expected. Expect West Virginia to score more.

The injury to starting quarterback Mason Heintschel is likely to really impact Pitt's season. An early game on the road at Boston College, which has played better of late, could spell trouble.

Yes, UTEP's 1-5 record isn't much to look at. There's no denying that. But the majority of these losses have come against quality teams. Don't be shocked if the Miners push for win No. 2.

Speaking of 1-5 teams, enter Rice. The Owls' lone win this season came over Houston Christian. Not ideal. The same can be said for Tulsa's three-game losing streak, which might stretch to four games after this one.

Army's two losses this season have come by a combined six points. FAU, meanwhile, has won four straight, although the strength of schedule can certainly be questioned. Army, owner of the nation's No. 1 rushing offense, keeps rolling.

articles.body:
Week 7 is the most important week of the 2026 college football season to date.

A pair of top-10 matchups in Bloomington and Provo headline a Saturday with six Top 25 showdowns.

The College Football Playoff hierarchy will change based on the results across those six contests, starting with the Ohio State Buckeyes' trip to face the Indiana Hoosiers.

Ohio State-Indiana is the only top-five clash on the docket and it will determine the favorite to win the Big Ten.

The Notre Dame Fighting Irish put their perfect record on the line against the BYU Cougars in one of two top-10 games they have this season.

BYU arguably has more to prove because of where it plays, and if pulls off the upset, it will cause a major rearrangement at the top of the rankings.

The weather is forecasted to be ideal for both of the top-10 clashes.

All of the updated forecasts for Week 7's biggest games can be found here on The Weather Channel.

No. 16 Mississippi State at No. 22 LSU (-14.5)

Prediction: LSU 34, Mississippi State 17

No. 6 Alabama (-7.5) at No. 14 Tennessee

Forecast: Chance of Showers. High of 87°F

No. 18 Oklahoma State at No. 20 Houston (-4.5)

Prediction: Houston 24, Oklahoma State 20

Prediction: Wake Forest 31, California 20

Ohio State plays its third Top 25 road game of the campaign in Bloomington on Saturday.

The Buckeyes fell to the Texas Longhorns in September and then beat the Iowa Hawkeyes two weeks ago.

The matchup with Indiana is the toughest game left on OSU's schedule now that the Oregon Ducks are out of the Top 25.

Saturday provides Indiana with its first real test of the season. The Hoosiers picked up six straight wins against unranked foes.

The Buckeyes are the more battle-tested team at this juncture of the season and they have the best player on either roster in wide receiver Jeremiah Smith.

The final result could come down to something as simple as how well Smith performed.

Julian Sayin has been the feeding the ball at will to the potential No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft. Smith has 916 receiving yards and 11 touchdowns. He had 164 yards against Texas and 206 yards versus Iowa.

Indiana's defense allows 188.5 passing yards per game and it ranks fifth in scoring defense at 11.8 points allowed per contest.

However, the Hoosiers haven't faced an offense as explosive as Ohio State's, so there's reason to be a little skeptical of those numbers.

Saturday is also a prove-it game for Hoosiers quarterback Josh Hoover. He has 17 passing touchdowns and zero interceptions, but he had five picks in two games against ranked teams with the TCU Horned Frogs last season.

Although Indiana is the reigning national champion, Ohio State is the more proven quantity at this point in the season. It's easier to trust the Buckeyes to win and gain control of the Big Ten title race.

Saturday's big primetime clash is all about BYU.

The Cougars play in the Big 12, which is viewed as a far weaker conference than the Big Ten and SEC, despite having three teams in the top 15.

BYU has an excellent home-field advantage in Provo, but it is a 10.5-point underdog and doesn't have star running back LJ Martin due to an injury.

The Cougars have also struggled in the last few weeks. They battled to get past TCU on the road two weeks ago and they weren't overly dominant against the Iowa State Cyclones last week at home.

Notre Dame comes to Utah with six double-digit wins on its resume. Its allowed over 13 points just once this season.

The Fighting Irish backed up all of the preseason hype around them, and no one would be surprised if they go into Provo and crush BYU.

A win, or even a close loss, for BYU would sway the national perspective of it as a CFB Playoff contender.

Moving the ball on the Notre Dame could be incredibly difficult for Bear Bachmeier and the Cougars.

The Irish have the allowed the fewest yards per game in the FBS and they have the fourth-best scoring defense.

articles.title: Can Oklahoma State make College Football Playoff? It's not a crazy path for Cowboys
articles.summary: Oklahoma State football has a clear path to the Big 12 title and a potential College Football Playoff spot.
articles.body:
STILLWATER — Oklahoma State's season-opening loss at Tulsa looks more mystifying by the week. All the Cowboys have done since then is win. Meanwhile, the Golden Hurricane is on a three-game skid.

Tulsa coach Tre Lamb is 2-0 against OSU and 1-9 in the American.

But, as Eric Morris and his Cowboys have done, maybe it's time we move on from the Tulsa debacle. Because guess what? It has no bearing on OSU contending for the Big 12 title, and thereby (probably) means a whole bunch of nothing when it comes to the Cowboys' not-so-crazy chances of making the College Football Playoff .

OSU's path to the playoff is straightforward: Make the Big 12 title game. Win the Big 12 title game. Whether that's by winning out or advancing to Arlington with a conference loss or two.

OSU has two big obstacles amid an otherwise soft conference schedule: vs. Texas Tech on Nov. 14, and at Houston at 6:30 p.m. Saturday. The Cowboys are slight underdogs against the Cougs. If OSU wins, as it did as underdogs against Oregon and at West Virginia, the Cowboys might be favored in every game the rest of the way. Including against Texas Tech, with it being in Stillwater and the Red Raiders not being the juggernaut they were a year ago.

Oklahoma State Cowboys vs UCF Knights in Week 6 college football, see our top photos

"It's not just one super team that's beating everyone," said junior defensive tackle Braylon Rigsby, one of two Texas Tech transfers (cornerback Mo Horn) on OSU's roster.

OSU's other five games: vs. Colorado, at Iowa State , at Kansas State , at Arizona State , vs. Kansas. The combined Big 12 record of those teams: 2-9.

The Big 12 has five teams without a conference win. OSU has played or will play four of the five.

There are also five Big 12 teams, including OSU, without a conference loss. Of the other four, OSU only plays Texas Tech. None of BYU, Utah or Baylor — a combined 7-0 in Big 12 play — are on the Cowboys' schedule.

Which is why this Houston game is so big. The Cougars' only loss was by two points at Texas Tech. Willie Fritz's bunch is a legitimate Big 12 contender , but the Cowboys could put two losses between them and the Cougars and own the head-to-head tiebreaker.

"This is where we want to be," Morris told his team this week. "These are the games that you dream about playing in … in these atmospheres and on national TV and all the things that come along with it."

It's a tiny sample, but the Big 12 has been a one-bid league in the two years of the expanded 12-team playoff. The conference champion has automatically gotten in, and that's it. Arizona State in 2024 and Texas Tech in 2025.

OSU linebacker Tate Romney was on that 2024 Arizona State team, which was picked to finish dead last in the preseason poll — a prediction so off that the Big 12 ceased conducting a preseason poll. These Cowboys came in with higher expectations, but they also carried the baggage of back-to-back winless Big 12 seasons.

The Big 12 isn't as deep or talented as the Big Ten or SEC, but it might be the best conference when you sort by unpredictability.

"Since I've been in the Big 12, it's almost been like that every single year," said Romney, now at his third Big 12 school.

A reminder of the playoff format: Each of the Power Four (ACC, Big 12, Big Ten, SEC) conference champions gets an automatic playoff bid. Then the highest-ranked team from the Group of Six ranks — conference champion or not — gets in. And there's a special clause for Notre Dame: If the Fighting Irish are in the top-12 of the committee's rankings, they're automatically in. So, without penciling in Notre Dame, there are seven at-large spots.

OSU's most likely path of snagging an at-large spot is by winning out in the regular season and losing in the Big 12 title game. That would include quality wins at Houston and vs. Texas Tech, and an Oregon win that's not looking as amazing.

But does a 10-2 OSU get in as an at-large? I don't see it. The Cowboys' conference schedule is too weak. And then there's the Tulsa loss. There will likely be 9-3 Big Ten and SEC teams with better resumes.

The Big 12's best chance of getting two teams in is BYU winning out in the regular season, thus netting a massive win over Notre Dame this weekend, and losing in the conference title game. In that case, a one-loss BYU would have a great chance of joining the conference champ in the playoff. Of course there are dozens of other scenarios. It's early. Probably too early to be talking about OSU making the playoff, but the Big 12 is gettable. And the Cowboys' path manageable.

Morris and the Mean Green were a win away from making the playoff last year. The North Texas Big Three of Drew Mestemaker, Caleb Hawkins and Wyatt Young are trying to position themselves for another shot having gone up a level.

"It's a great opportunity to show who we are, how good we are and for people to stop looking down on us like, 'Maybe they're good, maybe they're not,'" Young said. "No, we're a good team. We want to go prove that this week."

Joe Mussatto is a sports columnist for The Oklahoman. Have a story idea for Joe? Email him at jmussatto@oklahoman.com . Support Joe's work and that of other Oklahoman journalists by purchasing a digital subscription today at subscribe.oklahoman.com .
